chief_complaint: orbital blowout fracture with double vision when looking up and cheek numbness after softball strike to eye
hpi_details: 25F softball player struck directly in the left eye by a line-drive softball. Experienced immediate periorbital swelling and bruising. Presents to ED complaining of double vision (diplopia) specifically when trying to look upward, numbness over her left cheek and upper teeth, and a feeling that her left eye is slightly sunken inward.
ideas: thinks her eyeball was ruptured or permanently pushed backward into her skull
concerns: terrified of permanent double vision that will ruin her sports and daily life
expectations: wants emergency facial CT scan and surgical repair to release her trapped eye muscle

clinical_knowledge.topic: Left Orbital Floor Blowout Fracture with Inferior Rectus Muscle Entrapment and Infraorbital Nerve Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Left Orbital Floor Blowout Fracture with Inferior Rectus Muscle Entrapment and Infraorbital Nerve Injury is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Instruct patient strictly on sinus precautions (no nose blowing or Valsalva maneuvers to prevent orbital emphysema and blindness), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: orbital blowout fracture with double vision when looking up and cheek numbness after softball strike to eye

Key HPI features: 25F softball player struck directly in the left eye by a line-drive softball. Experienced immediate periorbital swelling and bruising. Presents to ED complaining of double vision (diplopia) specifically when trying to look upward, numbness over her left cheek and upper teeth, and a feeling that her left eye is slightly sunken inward.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 78, BP 118/76. Left eye shows severe periorbital ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage. Visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally; pupillary light reflexes normal without Marcus Gunn pupil (intact optic nerve). Extraocular motility testing reveals restricted elevation of the left eye above midline with vertical diplopia. Decreased pinprick sensation along left infraorbital nerve distribution (cheek, lateral nose, upper lip). Hertel exophthalmometry confirms 2 mm enophthalmos on left. Maxillofacial facial CT confirms a 1.5 x 1.2 cm orbital floor blowout fracture with entrapment/herniation of the inferior rectus muscle and orbital fat into the underlying maxillary sinus.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Left Orbital Floor Blowout Fracture with Inferior Rectus Muscle Entrapment and Infraorbital Nerve Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Flap ischemia or tissue necrosis.
management_principles: Instruct patient strictly on sinus precautions (no nose blowing or Valsalva maneuvers to prevent orbital emphysema and blindness)

Schedule urgent surgical exploration via transconjunctival or subciliary approach within 3-7 days (or within 24 hours if oculocardiac reflex bradycardia/nausea or white-eyed blowout trapdoor present in pediatric patient) for reduction of entrapped inferior rectus muscle and reconstruction of orbital floor defect using titanium mesh or porous polyethylene alloplastic implant
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 25F presenting with blunt trauma to left orbit resulting in vertical diplopia, infraorbital nerve hypesthesia, and enophthalmos.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 78, BP 118/76. Left eye shows severe periorbital ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage. Visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally; pupillary light reflexes normal without Marcus Gunn pupil (intact optic nerve). Extraocular motility testing reveals restricted elevation of the left eye above midline with vertical diplopia. Decreased pinprick sensation along left infraorbital nerve distribution (cheek, lateral nose, upper lip). Hertel exophthalmometry confirms 2 mm enophthalmos on left. Maxillofacial facial CT confirms a 1.5 x 1.2 cm orbital floor blowout fracture with entrapment/herniation of the inferior rectus muscle and orbital fat into the underlying maxillary sinus.
reference_soap.assessment: Left Orbital Floor Blowout Fracture with Inferior Rectus Muscle Entrapment and Infraorbital Nerve Injury.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange urgent ophthalmic and facial-trauma assessment, including visual acuity, pupils, ocular motility, and CT review. Advise sinus precautions while awaiting review. Antibiotics should follow the clinician's assessment of open injury, sinus involvement, allergies, and local protocol. Urgent repair is considered for entrapment, an oculocardiac reflex, vision-threatening findings, or a clinically significant defect after specialist evaluation.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical triad of orbital floor blowout fractures (vertical diplopia with restricted gaze elevation, infraorbital nerve paresthesia, enophthalmos)
Explain the mechanism of hydraulic vs buckling forces causing orbital floor or medial wall fractures while preserving the sturdy orbital rim
Recognize critical indications for emergent (<24 hr) vs delayed (3-7 day) surgical repair (specifically identifying the pediatric 'white-eyed trapdoor' fracture causing oculocardiac reflex)
Describe surgical approaches to the orbital floor and materials used for structural reconstruction (titanium mesh, porous polyethylene, autologous bone)

Bradycardia, nausea, or vomiting with restricted eye movement suggesting entrapment

must_ask.objective: Mechanism and timing of eye injury
must_ask.say: What hit your eye, and exactly when did this happen?
Do you see double, and is it worse when looking up or to the side?
Is your cheek or upper teeth numb or tingling?
Have you noticed any change in your vision, eye pain, or nausea and vomiting?
Have you had any prior eye problems, surgeries, or vision correction?

history.answer: I was hit directly in my left eye by a line-drive softball during practice two hours ago, and now I'm seeing double whenever I look up.
It happened all of a sudden about two hours ago when the softball hit me, and the swelling and double vision started immediately.
My left eye was hit, but the double vision only occurs when both eyes are open. If I cover either eye, the second image goes away.
No, my vision never went completely dark or blacked out. It has just stayed doubled whenever I glance upward.
Looking straight ahead is clear, and nothing looks blurry or distorted. Things only split into two separate images when I look up.
Both near and far objects are sharp looking straight ahead. The trouble only happens when I gaze upward, and I do not wear glasses.
No, I have not noticed any bothersome glare, halos around streetlights, or difficulty seeing in dim light.
No, I haven't seen any floating specks, flashes of light, or dark shadows resembling a curtain across my vision.
When I look up, one image sits directly on top of the other. The double vision completely disappears as soon as I close or cover either eye.
My left eyelid is swollen and heavy to open, but it does not droop on its own, it doesn't worsen in the evening, and I can chew and swallow easily.
My left eye socket throbs with a dull ache that turns quite sharp whenever I try to look up, and the white of my eye is filled with blood.
No, I don't have any headache, tenderness over my temples, jaw pain when chewing, or stiffness in my neck and shoulders.
No arm or leg weakness, no slurred speech, and no dizziness, though the left side of my cheek and upper teeth feel completely numb.
I was struck by the softball today, but I have never had any prior injuries to my eyes, face, or head before this.
No, I have never had high blood pressure or diabetes, and my routine physicals have always been normal.
No, I have no history of irregular heartbeats, heart rhythm issues, or carotid artery problems.
I do not have severe nearsightedness, glaucoma, or cataracts, and I have never undergone any eye surgery.
I don't take steroids, hydroxychloroquine, tuberculosis pills, or any medications that could affect eyesight.
No one in my family has glaucoma, macular degeneration, or any hereditary vision conditions.
I can't play softball or drive safely with this double vision, and I'm really terrified it will end my athletic career.
The left side of my cheek, the left side of my nose, and my upper left teeth and gums feel numb, exactly like dental freezing.
My left eyeball feels sunken backward into the socket compared to my right eye.
No, I haven't had any nausea or vomiting, and I didn't lose consciousness when the ball struck me.
I'm terrified that my eyeball might be ruptured or permanently pushed back into my skull.
I'm terrified of permanent double vision that will ruin my athletic career and normal life.
I want an emergency facial CT scan and surgery right away to release the trapped eye muscle.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses and have always been healthy.
I have never had any operations, and I have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine or tobacco products.
I only have one or two beers socially with my teammates on weekends.
I am a 25-year-old college student and varsity softball player living in an off-campus apartment.
My parents and my brother are all healthy with no major medical problems.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my cycles are always regular every 28 days.
There is no possibility of pregnancy; my partner and I consistently use condoms.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats/min, respiratory rate is 14 breaths/min, body temperature is 36.7 C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
Young athletic female in acute discomfort holding an ice pack against her left eye, alert and fully oriented.
Left eye exhibits marked periorbital ecchymosis, significant soft tissue edema, and prominent subconjunctival hemorrhage; the right eye is clear.

Visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally with normal pupillary reflexes and no afferent defect, but extraocular motility reveals restricted elevation of the left eye above midline with vertical diplopia and 2 mm of left enophthalmos.
Point tenderness and mild step-off sensation along the left inferior orbital rim and anterior maxillary sinus wall without palpable crepitus on the right.
Decreased pinprick and light touch sensation across the left infraorbital nerve distribution, including the left lower eyelid, cheek, lateral nose, and upper lip.
Cranial nerve examination is normal aside from restricted left eye elevation due to mechanical muscle tethering and left trigeminal second division numbness.
Nasal examination shows no septal hematoma or ongoing hemorrhage, and oral inspection confirms intact dentition with normal dental occlusion.
Bilateral superficial temporal arteries are easily palpable, soft, non-tender, and without nodularity.
